sources.inspected: Actual HTML body text: multiple nouns form one noun-like group; a following case particle applies to that group; noun-listing to is not a general connector between sentences.
sources.qualification: Conditional and quotative to are not declared ungrammatical because this noun-listing use does not connect ordinary verb clauses. The lesson is not evidence that to itself means only.

sources.inspected: Actual HTML body text: representative noun lists, noun-like grouping, optional following nado, and the introductory completeness contrast with to.
sources.qualification: Do not upgrade the introductory completeness contrast into a context-free exclusivity claim. Do not adopt the page's blanket prohibition on nado with people: TUFS lesson 095 itself supplies a personal-name example in its nado section. The new article neither teaches that prohibition nor substitutes plural tachi for exemplification.

sources.sections: Vたり、Vたりします explanation, points 1-4
sources.inspected: Actual HTML body text and examples: representative activities, ta-form plus ri including swimming's voiced dari, present/habitual and completed descriptions, and alternating actions or states.
sources.qualification: This paired introductory pattern does not prohibit a single example. Alternation does not require an additional unnamed third state. Single exemplification is checked separately against the modern dictionary entry.

sources.sections: Connective particles, I (te), III (tari/shi), IV (node/kara), and VI (conditional to)
sources.inspected: Actual HTML body, including its account of several relationships expressed with te and a parallel-facts shi example. It explicitly notes that teaching tari as an inflected form and classifying it as a particle are different grammatical treatments.
sources.qualification: Te is not assigned an invariably chronological or exhaustive-list meaning. Shi is not confined to causal reasons. No claim is made that all frameworks assign these constructions the same part of speech.

sources.sections: AくてA・NAでNA・NでN, attachment explanations and the cause/reason extension
sources.inspected: Explanations of i-adjective kute, na-adjective and noun de, mixed predicates, and a connection expressing a reason rather than chronology.
sources.qualification: The page's categorical same-evaluation restriction is not adopted as a general rule. This article introduces basic affirmative connections, not the complete inflection system.

sources.sections: II (mo), VI (nado), VII (demo), and XI (combination with case particles)
sources.inspected: Actual HTML body: additive inclusion; nado with a single noun, activities and a category modifier; example-giving and softening; dismissive nado; demo in a drink suggestion and a distinct even/minimum case; combination of focus and case particles.
sources.qualification: Addition, exemplification, dismissive stance and even are not collapsed into one sense. Named examples do not certify every authored scenario. Nado's personal-name example also limits the overly broad people restriction on lesson 048.

sources.sections: と‐か [rengo], second subdivision sense 1 and its supplement; first subdivision and second subdivision sense 2 as boundaries
sources.inspected: Actual named dictionary text: exemplary coordination of things and actions; possible omission of final toka; separate uncertain-reporting and assertion-softening uses. Adjacent homographs and dialect/name entries were excluded.
sources.qualification: The source supports clause attachment and omission, not unrestricted interchangeability with ya or a claim that every clause-final toka is listing.

sources.sections: Modern たり [connective particle], sense 1a parallel actions/states, 1b alternation, sense 2 exemplification, and supplement
sources.inspected: Actual named dictionary text, separate from the preceding historical auxiliaries: parallel actions/states, alternation between opposites, and an individual example implying comparable possibilities.
sources.qualification: The article does not turn the common paired teaching form into a mandatory count of two, equate the ta-shaped form with past event time, or present all conversational omissions as one beginner pattern. Historical auxiliaries and the person-counting suffix are outside scope.

sources.inspected: Actual named dictionary text: parallel/contrasted facts, causal grounds including a single shi and a polite predicate, and sentence-final suspension of a fact/condition with an implied conclusion.
sources.qualification: No mandatory hidden second reason, uniform causal reading or guaranteed soft/polite tone is inferred. The preceding historical auxiliaries, later homographs, regional dictionary and automatically generated examples are not the evidence.

sources.sections: Expressing multiple reasons using shi; expressing multiple actions or states using tari-suru
sources.inspected: English attachment explanations: da after affirmative nonpast nouns/na-adjectives before shi; past-shaped verb/adjective/noun forms plus ri; inflected suru and negative examples.
sources.qualification: Simplified extraction omits Japanese from many examples; missing strings were not reconstructed or treated as inspected examples. Do not adopt an invariably chronological te, always sentence-final suru, or a claim that only final suru can carry negation. Per-item negative tari and the entire predicate have distinct scopes.

sources.inspected: English explanations of noun coordination versus accompaniment and the more colloquial register of toka.
sources.qualification: The broad and/or gloss and unrestricted sameness of ya/toka are not adopted. Japanese examples omitted by simplified extraction are not counted as inspected. Unrelated claims about explanatory no and gender are outside this article.

sources.sections: へいりつ‐じょし [parallel particles], definition and modern inventory
sources.inspected: Actual named dictionary definition: joining words on an equal footing, often using forms otherwise classified as case, focus or connective particles; inventory includes to, ni, ka, ya, yara and dano.
sources.qualification: This is evidence for a broader category, not a complete attachment or tone guide for each advanced pattern. Adjacent regional/Wikipedia material was not used to establish standard usage.

priorEvidence.use: Reuse the published category-example/resemblance distinction for you-na, additive hoka and ue-ni, and the distinction between noun, conditional and concessive connections. Read the relevant formal-noun sections and current noni article; consult the existing records for navigation. This is not a fresh external audit of every linked article or historical source.

core: Noun to versus representative ya/toka/nado, including group scope and following particles.
Single nado, toka, tari and shi; a single demo suggestion and additive mo as neighboring uses.
Tari formation, tense context, per-item versus whole-predicate negation, and alternating states.
Shi attachment across predicate types, polite/plain connections, additive facts, reasons and an unstated conclusion.
Te/kute/de connections, both/neither mo, noun alternatives with ka, and example-giving demo.
Links to you-na, hoka and ue-ni, plus a brief recognition-only advanced map.
remainingScope: Learning-effectiveness measurement, unrestricted connector selection, clausal toka, suspended sentence-final shi, full shi/register paradigms and verb te formation.
Full treatment of yara, dano, nari, noun-listing ni, formal conjunctions and their legal drafting distinctions.
Detailed nanka/nante, reporting toka, conversational omissions, sentence-final tone and dialects.
A complete inflection curriculum, exhaustive paraphrase coverage, or a single universal grammatical classification.

answerPolicy: Three noun lists accept to/ya/toka with neutral or representative framing explicitly allowed.
Three single-noun examples accept nado/toka; two invitations accept demo/nado/toka.
The short-connector pool and case-particle requirements are visible before answering.
Formation drills explicitly request tari, short plain shi, or basic affirmative te/de; kana/kanji variants and fitting fuller tari copulas are accepted.
Twelve meaning tasks define their labels and readings before answering; they are not connector-production tasks or a universal grammatical taxonomy.
Base options remain one-correct for older clients. Existing choose-any presentation can add a second correct button on eligible appearances; typed acceptance is not limited to displayed options.

authoringNotes: Exhaustive versus non-exhaustive is a useful teaching contrast, not a proof that to alone excludes every other item. Explicit dake and a following negative sentence demonstrate actual exclusion.
One example is not a defective multi-item list. Tari alternation also need not imply a third unnamed state, and shi need not guarantee a second reason.
Preserve overlap without manufacturing exclusive answers: ya/toka and shi/kara can both fit while changing register or framing.

Examples are original illustrations or short conventional grammatical forms, not copied source exercises. Sources support constructions; the author must still check complete sentences, readings and translations.
Do not treat the TUFS nado-with-people prohibition as universal, or use stripped Japanese examples as source evidence.
Keep learner links inside imported article folders or direct HTTPS sources. Contributor provenance stays in docs and is not linked as an app page.

reconciliation.originalConcern: The short distractor feedback described a tari connection without explaining that attaching the offered だったり to the printed 行かない is malformed. The longer explanation already rejected inserting だ after ない, so this was nonblocking.
reconciliation.before: A たり connection, not the plain し connection requested.
reconciliation.after: 行かないだったり is malformed: だったり cannot attach to 行かない. Negative たり would require rewriting it as 行かなかったり; this blank asks for し.

reasoning.correctness: The new feedback correctly distinguishes the malformed literal completion from a properly reformulated negative tari item. 行かない has past-negative form 行かなかった; adding り gives 行かなかったり, not 行かないだったり. This is an item-internal negative formation, not a claim that final-negative tari expressions have only one possible shape.
reasoning.scopedCoverage: The rationale now covers both defects relevant to this option: attachment to the printed predicate and failure to supply the explicitly requested plain し connection. It explicitly calls the tari example a rewrite, so it does not suggest that 行かなかったり can be inserted after the unchanged printed 行かない.
reasoning.comprehensibility: A learner reading only this option's feedback can now see why the literal distractor fails and why a grammatical tari reformulation still is not this blank's answer. The accepted completion remains 行かないし.

reconciliation.originalConcern: The twelve meaning-label tasks repeated unnecessarily long setup prose and redundant period-plus-semicolon definition boundaries. Shortening was optional and had to preserve definitions, the task-type warning, and decisive scenario information before answering.

reasoning.correctness: All three label definitions and their kana readings are retained in every affected translation. The only definition changes are removal of the two redundant boundary periods before semicolons. Every decisive English scenario is exactly unchanged. Fresh contextual assessment of all twelve tasks establishes no new competing accepted class.
reasoning.scopedCoverage: All twelve translations still begin with 'Choose a meaning label, not a connector (kana accepted).' The first six explicitly classify the whole quote, including final polarity and stated opposites. The last six explicitly classify the quoted connector's relation; their prompts name し or のに, and the definitions still describe the relation between one fact and the following judgment or situation.
reasoning.comprehensibility: The shortened setup makes the task type and classification scope easier to locate without removing necessary distinctions. Removing 'between the clauses, not every fact in the sentence' from the relation-task boilerplate is not a consequential loss: 'quoted connector's relation', the connector-specific prompt, relational definitions, and retained scenario restrictions jointly preserve that scope.

changedExerciseAssessments.assessment: The printed negative predicate takes し directly. The new rationale correctly marks 行かないだったり as malformed and labels 行かなかったり as a rewrite rather than a completion of the existing blank. The visible short-plain-form drill and unchanged answer remain decisive.

Taking photos remains one affirmed example on days off. The whole-quote instruction and retained definition exclude an opposite pair and denial; final します remains positive. Shortening does not turn this into a connector-production task.

Books remain an affirmed noun example among things put in the bag. The unchanged scenario and definition neither impose an exhaustive list nor describe opposite occasions or denial. The retained whole-quote instruction supports 例示.

The unchanged sometimes-cooking/sometimes-not scenario and したり、しなかったりします affirm variation across occasions. The explicit instruction to include final polarity and stated opposites prevents mistaking item-internal negation for denial of the whole activity.

Stopping and moving remain stated opposing actions in an ongoing repeated pattern. The definition and whole-quote scope still distinguish this from a single affirmative example or denial. No new third-state requirement is introduced.

Final しません still denies doing the example activity at night. The time restriction is unchanged, and the retained final-polarity instruction excludes an affirmative sometimes-playing/sometimes-not interpretation. The classification concerns the whole quote, not the exemplifying function of たり in isolation.

The unchanged scenario denies reading manga during work, not all reading at all times. Final negation and the preserved whole-quote instruction continue to distinguish 否定 from an affirmed varying pattern.

The retained scenario explicitly says the two preferences are simply reported, neither causal nor surprising. Different preferences alone do not establish the defined contrary-expectation relation. The prompt names し, so the shortened relational instruction still selects 追加 rather than requiring classification of every fact.

The retained scenario reports two opening statuses rather than one opening causing the other. The prompt asks about the quoted し and the setup explicitly asks for its relation. An imagined later outing could use both facts as reasons, but that unstated larger story is still not the requested relation between these clauses.

The stopped rain is still explicitly offered as support for the following walking proposal. The retained definition and scenario make this a reason relation, not merely two independent facts or a proposal contrary to expectation. The question still identifies the relation of し, not a unique replacement connector.

Hunger remains explicitly offered as the reason for the lunch proposal. The quoted-connector scope and unchanged supporting-reason definition retain 理由 without requiring a second stated reason or judging another possible connector.

The unchanged scenario explicitly presents remaining sleepy as contrary to the speaker's expectation after going to bed early. The prompt names のに and the retained definition classifies this relation as 逆接; no universal guarantee about early bedtime or causal reading is introduced.

Turning on the heating versus a still-cold room remains explicitly contrary to expectation in the scenario. The named のに and retained relational definition continue to select 逆接, not a mere list of two facts or a claim that heating caused the cold.
